summary: Scribes and Pharisees bring Jesus a woman caught in adultery to trap Him; He turns the question on their consciences and sends her away uncondemned, to sin no more.
key_insight: Jesus set one condition for throwing the first stone: “He who is without sin among you.” Only one person in that court met it, and He was the one who said, “Neither do I condemn you.”
story: Everyone went home, but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early the next morning He came again into the temple. All the people came to Him, and He sat down and taught them.

Then the scribes and Pharisees brought in a woman caught in adultery and stood her in the middle of the crowd. “Teacher,” they said, “this woman was caught in adultery, in the very act. Now Moses, in the law, commanded us that such should be stoned. But what do You say?” They said this to test Him, hoping for something to accuse Him of.

Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with His finger, as though He had not heard them. When they kept on asking, He straightened up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first.” Then He stooped down again and wrote on the ground.

Those who heard it were convicted by their conscience. They went out one by one, beginning with the oldest, until the last of them was gone. Jesus was left alone, with the woman still standing where they had set her.

Jesus straightened up and, seeing no one but the woman, said to her, “Woman, where are those accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?” She said, “No one, Lord.” And Jesus said to her, “Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more.”

scene.label: The manuscripts
scene.text: The NKJV includes John 7:53–8:11 and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts do not have it.

scene.label: The trap
scene.text: If Jesus said to let her go, He could be charged with setting aside the law of Moses. If He said to stone her, He would contradict His welcome of sinners and could be accused before Rome, which kept the power of execution for itself (John 18:31).

scene.label: What the law required
scene.text: The law did call for death in cases of adultery, but for both the man and the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). She was caught “in the very act,” yet the man is nowhere in the scene.

scene.label: The first stone
scene.text: Under the law, the witnesses were to throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus did not deny the law. He asked who among the accusers was fit to begin.

scene.label: Writing on the ground
scene.text: John does not say what Jesus wrote, and every answer is a guess. Some point to Jeremiah 17:13, where those who depart from the Lord “shall be written in the earth.”

witnesses.john: In John the account stands between the Feast of Tabernacles and Jesus’ words, “I am the light of the world.” It shows in one scene what John records Jesus saying: God sent His Son not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17). The leaders judge “according to the flesh” (8:15); Jesus sees both the sin and the sinner, and deals truly with each.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is holy and merciful at once. He does not excuse the woman’s sin or set aside the law, yet He, the only one without sin, refuses to condemn her and calls her to a new life.
seeing.living: Jesus spoke in a set order: “Neither do I condemn you” first, then “go and sin no more.” His mercy is not permission, and His call to holiness is not cruelty. Receive the first word, and live by the second.
seeing.ponder: Are you more often the one holding a stone or the one standing in the middle, and what does Jesus say to you there?

preaching.big_idea: The only one without sin chose mercy, and His mercy calls us to sin no more.
outline: A standard that silenced the accusers (8:7–9)
A word of mercy and a call to holiness (8:10–11)
preaching.watch_for: Watch the posture: Jesus sits to teach, stoops to write, and twice raises Himself to speak (8:2, 6–8, 10). The accusers stand over the woman, but in the end only Jesus and she remain, and He is the one with the right to condemn.
